headline: Funding closes; delivery and cash remain the next test
bullets: IREN reports $200m AI Cloud revenue, while its >$4bn ARR target slips into 2027. Expansion still needs financing beyond a narrowly funded program.
Microsoft confirms $25bn issuance and Meta $15bn dollar closing. Meta’s €9bn notes await delivery; the common-forward option does not mean immediate cash.
Google’s site acquisition, PPL’s nonbinding power terms and Equinix’s SG6 opening are different milestones—not interchangeable operating AI capacity.

articles.title: IREN revenue grows; the buildout still needs delivery and cash
articles.source_name: IREN and infrastructure issuers - dated primary disclosures
articles.observation: IREN reports $200m of AI revenue. Other announcements mark site ownership, conditional future power and an opened data-centre phase.
articles.summary: These are distinct steps toward delivered, paid capacity.
articles.implication: Growing sales and opened sites strengthen the buildout case. Customer acceptance, usable power and collections still determine whether commitments become returns.
articles.beneficiaries: Cloud operators, power developers and equipment suppliers can benefit as contracted projects reach acceptance, billing and payment.
articles.risks: Commissioning delays, incomplete funding, power constraints and weak occupancy can extend the gap between investment and returns.
articles.counterevidence: Recognized revenue, customer prepayments, a site acquisition and SG6 opening show concrete progress; the evidence does not support a blanket claim that every project is unfunded or stalled.
articles.confirms: Accepted capacity, occupied cabinets, binding power agreements, received financing and recurring collections would strengthen the conversion case.
articles.refutes: Slipping delivery, failed funding conditions, customer cancellations or poor take-up of opened capacity would weaken expected returns.
articles.uncertainty: IREN backlog is not collections, and its 86% segment margin excludes depreciation and site costs. Site-level utilization and downstream AI returns remain undisclosed.

articles.title: Marvell–Lumentum deal: sales growth adds operating evidence
articles.observation: The companies announced a definitive all-stock acquisition agreement: 4.500 Marvell shares per Lumentum share, with approximately $115 billion implied enterprise value.
articles.summary: Lumentum’s same-day results add an operating checkpoint: $1.2626 billion quarterly revenue and management-disclosed purchase commitments above $5 billion for a second major near-packaged/co-packaged optics win. The proposed merger still targets closing in the first half of 2028.
articles.implication: Existing sales and purchase commitments give the optics thesis more substance. Their conversion into collected cash and delivered products matters separately from the all-stock acquisition value.
articles.claim_type: Issuer-disclosed agreement and unaudited results; commitments attributed to management; guidance and merger benefits are expectations; implications are analysis
articles.beneficiaries: AI infrastructure customers could gain more integrated chips and optical products; suppliers benefit only as customer demand converts into qualified shipments and collections.
articles.risks: Manufacturing constraints, customer order changes and weak cash conversion could limit the optics ramp. Regulatory or shareholder rejection and integration disruption could prevent merger benefits.
articles.counterevidence: Quarter-end cash and short-term investments fell $758.8 million. The release supplies no cash-flow statement or shipment-unit counts. Marvell’s preliminary fiscal Q3 revenue midpoint remained unchanged, and neither the merger nor the new optics commitments establish incremental cash receipts.
articles.confirms: Conversion of optics commitments into delivered revenue and cash, production progress, customer-qualified joint products and required merger approvals would support the thesis.
